correctness.rationale: Exact centered-write-noise second moments yield a diagonal squared-error quadratic form. Strict convexity in eigenvalue proves only spectral endpoints can dominate. Both unique roots exist by monotone functions; their branch structure proves one global minimizer. A Descartes one-sign-change cubic proves the unique parameter phase boundary. The 2x2 rational counterexample and SNR calculation are exact. The included standard-library checker verifies 1056 individual finite assertions; the universal claims rely on the analytic argument.

evidence: Shah et al. (2026), Section 3.3 gives a more general SPD shifted-target SNR condition, but not a minimax true-inverse-risk solution. Etter and Ying (2022) allow general random input matrices but optimize a different matrix estimator and norm.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Greater matrix generality is not stronger coverage when the loss or random mechanism differs. The current diagonal specialization includes an exact optimality and phase comparison not implied by either general result.

originality.rationale: The primary source gives an SNR threshold for implementing the shifted target plus a separate bias formula, not the minimax total true-inverse risk or its unique stationary/crossing phase diagram. Prior general operator-shifting theory uses a different estimator and noise distribution. Indexed relevant findings also optimize different risk functions or noise mechanisms; no known statement implies the exact cubic frontier and the infeasible-but-optimal shift example. Historical completeness is unproved.
residual_risks: Published indexed mathematical findings were not all accessible as full packages; only returned title/claim summaries could be compared.
Unindexed or inaccessible older literature could contain an equivalent result.
Optimization and SNR statements are for a deliberately simplified diagonal block, not arbitrary SPD bases or deployed hardware.

value.rationale: The programming shift is an explicit natural design variable in the underlying model. Its best true-solution approximation shift differs in a provable, sharp region from what implementation-only SNR feasibility would suggest, so the theorem gives a nontrivial decision boundary and a false-equivalence counterexample. Scope is restricted, and it does not imply solver speedup or realistic-hardware advantage.
